title: Itza Mayans
capsule: The Itza were a Maya-speaking people of probable Chontal origin who established their capital at Nojpetén (modern Flores) on an island in Lake Petén Itzá in northern Guatemala, emerging as an independent polity after Spanish conquest bypassed the Petén lowlands. Their kingdom, Kan Ek' (named after the ruling title), preserved Classic Maya traditions in governance, architecture, and long-count calendar knowledge long after the collapse of the northern lowland cities. Spanish military expeditions under Martín de Ursúa y Arizmendi finally captured Nojpetén on 13 March 1697, killing or enslaving the last independent Itza population and ending the last sovereign Maya state.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The Itza kingdom's core territory around Lake Petén Itzá is well attested by Spanish colonial accounts and archaeology; the extent of its tributary hinterland is less precisely defined.
